input.summary: The workflow keeps the CI hardening: actions pinned to SHAs, persist-credentials false, a read-only default, and tag names passed through env with no template injection. But it signs in the same job and on the same runner that just compiled and ran third-party code (build scripts, proc macros, and unpinned cargo-install tools), with a restored build cache and the contents: write token in the job. Anything that runs during the build can wait on the runner and take the private key and passphrase in the Sign step. The README's verify steps also let a swapped, unsigned SHA256SUMS pass, and they don't name the key to trust. cargo test: 9 passed, 1 ignored; the YAML parses.

findings.comment: Building, signing and publishing all happen in one job. Earlier steps in that job run untrusted code: cargo install of unpinned crates, every dependency's build.rs and proc macros, and code from a restored cache. That code runs as the same user on the same runner, so it can leave something behind that the Sign step then runs: a gpg wrapper earlier in PATH, or changes under ~/.cargo/bin or $HOME. It can also watch /proc while the Sign step runs and read GPG_PRIVATE_KEY and GPG_PASSPHRASE from its environment. The job's write permission is also wider than the build needs.
findings.fix: Split it into three jobs. `build`: permissions contents: read, no secrets; runs `just deb` and uploads target/debian/*.deb with actions/upload-artifact (pinned SHA). `sign`: needs build, contents: read, `environment: release`; no checkout, no cache, no cargo; uses the preinstalled /usr/bin/gpg by absolute path; downloads the artifact, signs it, and uploads the signed set. `publish`: needs sign, contents: write; only runs `gh release create`.

findings.comment: The release job restores Swatinem/rust-cache, and any run on the default branch may have written that cache. A poisoned target/ or ~/.cargo, from a compromised dependency or a malicious build script on main, then gets into the signed artifact and the job that holds the signing key. This is the cache-poisoning pattern: release builds should never use shared caches.
findings.fix: Remove the rust-cache step from release.yml, so the release is built clean. If you keep a cache, set `save-if: false` and only use it in the secret-free build job after the split; clean is still better.

findings.comment: `cargo install --locked just cargo-deb` installs whatever versions are newest at release time, and they run in the release job. A compromised new release of either crate, or of one of their dependencies, would run with the key still to come in this job. Dependabot doesn't track these crates.
findings.fix: Pin exact versions, e.g. `cargo install --locked just@<x.y.z> cargo-deb@<x.y.z>`, matching the version the README says it was checked with. Run them only in the secret-free build job.

findings.comment: The GPG secrets are repository secrets. Any workflow run on a push to any branch can read them, so anyone with write access can push a branch with a changed workflow and print the key. Nothing gates who can trigger signing either: any pushed `v*` tag signs and publishes.
findings.fix: Put GPG_PRIVATE_KEY, GPG_PASSPHRASE and GPG_KEY_ID in a `release` environment whose deployment rule allows only `v*` tags, ideally with a required reviewer. Use `environment: release` on the signing job only. Add a tag ruleset protecting `v*`. Change the README's secrets section to say environment secrets, not repository secrets.

findings.comment: `gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.asc && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS` checks the signature on SHA256SUMS.asc, then checks the hashes in a separate, unsigned SHA256SUMS. Someone who can replace release assets can keep the genuine .asc, swap the .deb, and supply a matching SHA256SUMS, and both commands still succeed. Separately, `gpg --verify` accepts a valid signature from any key in the user's keyring, and the README never says which key the releases are signed with.
findings.fix: Hash-check the content that was signed: `gpg --decrypt SHA256SUMS.asc | sha256sum -c --ignore-missing -`, or use `gpgv --keyring ./nightlight.gpg --output - SHA256SUMS.asc | sha256sum -c -`. Publish the signing key's full fingerprint in the README, and say how to get the public key: commit the public key, e.g. as data/signing-key.asc, or name a keyserver. Tell users to check the fingerprint gpg reports matches it.

findings.comment: The temporary keyring and the gpg-agent holding the unlocked key are only cleaned up when every step succeeds: with set -e, a failed sign or verify skips line 84. gpg-agent also keeps running after `rm -rf`.
findings.fix: Right after mktemp, add `trap 'gpgconf --kill gpg-agent; rm -rf "${GNUPGHOME}"' EXIT`, and remove the trailing rm -rf.

text:
I've asked for changes to Engineer 1's signed release workflow before it merges. The main problem is that the signing key is exposed to code the build runs.

What it gets right: the workflow follows the existing CI setup (actions pinned to full SHAs, `persist-credentials: false`, read-only permissions by default), and the tag name is passed in safely. The project's tests pass (9 passed, 1 skipped) and the workflow file parses. I haven't run the workflow itself on GitHub.

Five things must be fixed:
- **Signing happens next to the build:** one job builds, signs and publishes. The build runs third-party code: dependency build scripts and the `just` and `cargo-deb` tools it installs. That code can leave something on the runner that steals `GPG_PRIVATE_KEY` and `GPG_PASSPHRASE` in the signing step. The fix is three jobs: build (no secrets), sign (no build, cache or cargo), and publish (the only one allowed to write).
- **The release reuses a shared build cache:** a poisoned cache would end up in the signed `.deb`. Drop the cache step from the release workflow.
- **The install tools aren't pinned:** `cargo install` fetches whatever versions of `just` and `cargo-deb` are newest at release time. Pin exact versions.
- **The signing secrets are repository secrets:** anyone who can push a branch can read them, and pushing any `v*` tag signs and publishes. Move them into a `release` environment that only `v*` tags can use, protect `v*` tags, and change the README to match.
- **The README's verify steps can be fooled:** they check the signature on `SHA256SUMS.asc`, then check the hashes in a separate, unsigned `SHA256SUMS` that someone could swap along with the `.deb`. The checksum step should use the signed content. The README also never gives the signing key's fingerprint, so a valid signature from any key in the user's keyring would pass.

One should fix: the temporary keyring is only deleted if every step succeeds, and the gpg process holding the unlocked key keeps running afterwards. A cleanup that runs on exit fixes both.

Build, sign and publish now run as separate jobs, with no cache, pinned tools, environment secrets, a cleanup trap, and the key published with a fingerprint slot in the README. #5 is only partly fixed: the new verify command still passes a tampered checksum file. findings.comment: `gpg --decrypt SHA256SUMS.asc | sha256sum -c --ignore-missing -` doesn't stop on a bad signature. gpg writes the clear-signed text to stdout even when the signature is BAD or the key is unknown, and the pipeline's exit status is sha256sum's. I tested it: I edited a hash in SHA256SUMS.asc to match a swapped .deb, gpg printed 'BAD signature', and the command still printed 'a.deb: OK' and exited 0. So a forged SHA256SUMS.asc with a matching swapped .deb passes, which is the attack #5 was about. The only guard is the sentence asking users to read gpg's stderr. The command also accepts any key in the user's keyring.
findings.fix: Verify against the release key alone, and hash-check only if that succeeds. For example: `gpg --dearmor < signing-key.asc > signing-key.gpg` once, after checking the fingerprint. Then `gpgv --keyring ./signing-key.gpg --output SHA256SUMS.verified SHA256SUMS.asc && sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS.verified`. I checked that gpgv exits 1 on the tampered file, so `&&` stops the hash check. Add a note that SHA256SUMS.verified must not be used if gpgv failed. Do the same for the .deb: `gpgv --keyring ./signing-key.gpg cosmic-ext-nightlight_*.deb.asc cosmic-ext-nightlight_*.deb`.

text:
I've asked for changes again. All but one of the earlier problems are fixed; the one left is in the README's instructions for checking a download.

**Fixed:**
- Building, signing and publishing now run as three separate jobs. Only the signing job gets the key, and only the publishing job can write to the repository.
- The release no longer uses a shared build cache.
- `just` and `cargo-deb` are pinned to exact versions (1.59.0 and 3.8.0).
- The signing secrets are now meant to live in a protected `release` environment, and the README explains how to set that up.
- The key is cleaned up after signing even when a step fails.
- The public key is attached to each release.

**Still to fix:** the new check, `gpg --decrypt SHA256SUMS.asc | sha256sum -c --ignore-missing -`, still accepts a tampered checksum file. When the signature is bad, gpg prints "BAD signature" but still passes the text on, and the command succeeds. I tried it locally: I edited a hash to match a swapped `.deb`, and the command printed `OK` and exited 0. That's the forged-download attack this fix was meant to stop.

The fix is to check against the release key alone with `gpgv`, and only check the hashes if that succeeds (`gpgv … && sha256sum -c …`). I tested that `gpgv` fails on the tampered file, so the hash check never runs.

**Your step:** the README's fingerprint is a placeholder. You'll need to fill it in before the first release, since you're the one who knows the key.

text:
I've approved Engineer 1's signed release workflow; nothing left from my review needs fixing before it merges.

- **Checking a download:** the README now verifies the checksum file against the release key alone with `gpgv`, and only checks the hashes if that succeeds. The `.deb`'s own signature is checked the same way. Last round I tested this approach on a tampered checksum file: `gpgv` failed and the hash check never ran. I didn't run the README's commands as written this time.
- **The placeholder fingerprint:** the engineer left this to you, which is right, because only you know the signing key. Until the README has the real fingerprint, the release workflow stops before building, so no tagged release can go out without it.

**Before the first release:** put the key's full fingerprint in the README. Then set up the `release` environment in the repository's GitHub settings: add the three GPG secrets to it, limit it to `v*` tags, and add a required reviewer. Also add a rule protecting `v*` tags.
